title: Why is sea water salty?
subtitle: Oceans
subject: sciences
description: One liter of seawater contains approximately 35 grams of salt. This salt has accumulated over billions of years. Here's where it comes from.

hero.hook: The rivers are gentle. The oceans are salty. The secret is time and evaporation.

blocks.text: Oceans cover more than **70%** of the planet. On average, one liter of seawater contains approximately **35 grams of salt**. This is not a coincidence: it is the result of a very long process.
Salt does not “fall” from the sky ready-made. It travels from the continents, then becomes trapped in the ocean.

sections.title: Salt comes first from the earth

blocks.text: Rain, passing through the air, picks up a little carbon dioxide. It becomes slightly acidic. As it falls on the rocks, it gently attacks them: this is **chemical erosion**.

blocks.caption: Salt marshes: evaporation concentrates the salt dissolved in seawater.

blocks.text: The rivers then carry dissolved minerals, especially **sodium** and **chlorine**, the two ingredients of table salt. They dump them into the sea.
Underwater volcanoes and hot springs on the ocean floor also add salts. But the main part still comes from the continents.
Good question: if the rivers bring salt, why is the water of the Rhône or the Seine not salty? Because the salt there is very diluted, and because the water in the rivers is constantly renewed.

In the ocean, it's different. Under the Sun, water **evaporates** and returns to the sky. The salt, **remains**. Year after year, century after century, it accumulates. We call it . [[Hydrological cycle and salt accumulation]]

Salt water is more **dense** (“heavier” for the same volume) than fresh water. At the poles, when surface water freezes, salt is partly released into the surrounding liquid water. This water becomes even denser and plunges to the bottom.
This movement helps drive large ocean currents. These currents transport heat and nutrients around the globe. Salt is not just a matter of taste: it is part of the planet's climate engine.

Salinity is not the same everywhere. Near the equator, strong evaporation can concentrate salt. Near large rivers or melting ice floes, the water is softer. The Dead Sea is an extreme case: very little water leaves, a lot of salt remains.
Sea water is salty because rivers bring minerals from the continents, and evaporation leaves the salt in the ocean. This accumulation has been going on for billions of years.
